source.title: Scaling Laws For Scalable Oversight
source.authors: Joshua Engels; David D. Baek; Subhash Kantamneni; Max Tegmark

page_placements.theme: Scalable-oversight games: Guard and Houdini Elo against general capability, and nested oversight success

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses weak-to-strong generalization but explicitly distinguishes its work from that literature: its experiments study oversight games without training, not fine-tuning a strong student on weak labels or measuring PGR.
record.gate_note: The paper reports model performance scaling in Mafia, Debate, Backdoor Code, and Wargames, but these are interactive oversight games rather than the weak-label fine-tuning intervention or PGR in the claim. The paper says that applying its framework to fine-tuning with weak labels is left for future work. Game results are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates prompted LLMs in oversight games (Mafia, Debate, Backdoor Code, Wargames) and fits game Elo against Chatbot Arena Elo. No strong model is fine-tuned on weaker-model labels and no PGR is reported. The authors separate their work from weak-to-strong generalization, saying they focus on protocols that do not require training. They leave the weak-label fine-tuning game to future work. The game results measure a related but different construct: oversight and deception win rates between capability-mismatched models. They do not measure a student surpassing its supervisor's labels.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find that oversight-game performance scales with general capability at slopes and intercepts that vary by game. They estimate low NSO success rates at a 400 Elo gap for most games and recommend designing protocols where the Guard slope exceeds the Houdini slope. Weak-label fine-tuning is left for future work.
record.recipe_differences: No weak-label fine-tuning recipe is used. The study evaluates prompted LLMs in oversight games and models game Elo as a function of general Elo.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling trends vary by game and dataset: Debate is mostly flat on BoolQ, while judge performance scales on TruthfulQA, QuaLITY, and PrOntoQA; Guard and Houdini trends also differ across games.

fits_no_version.finding: In Mafia, Guard and Houdini domain Elo both scale roughly linearly with general Elo. The Guard slope is steeper.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In Mafia, detection ability scales with general capability faster than deception ability.

fits_no_version.finding: In Debate, judge Elo scales with general Elo on TruthfulQA, QuaLITY and PrOntoQA, while debater Elo stays flat. Both roles are mostly flat on BoolQ.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In LLM debate, judge performance scales with capability but debater performance does not, depending on the dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: In Backdoor Code, the Houdini slope is steeper than the nearly flat Guard slope, and the Guard intercept is higher. Given a viable backdoor, stronger Houdinis do not evade detection more often.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Capability gains help produce valid backdoors more than detect them, but do not make backdoors more deceptive.

fits_no_version.finding: In Wargames, Guard Elo rises with general Elo while Houdini Elo is mostly constant.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In roleplay containment games, monitor performance scales with capability while escape performance does not.

fits_no_version.finding: Under the fitted Elo curves, nested scalable oversight success at a 400-point general Elo gap is estimated at 13.5% (Mafia), 51.7% (Debate), 10.0% (Backdoor Code) and 9.4% (Wargames).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multi-step weak-to-strong oversight success probability falls with the capability gap, at rates that depend on the game.

record.problems: The paper identifies the oversight settings as simplified and notes that Wargames roleplay differs from actual escape; deception is induced by prompting rather than fine-tuning. Chatbot Arena Elo is an imperfect proxy for general intelligence. The reported game scaling findings are mainly qualitative in the text, with detailed curves in figures.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant rows were omitted. The paper's NSO success-rate estimates and theoretical optimization results concern its game-based model, not weak-label fine-tuning or PGR.

untested.parts: All: no weak-label fine-tuning, no comparison of a student with its weak supervisor, no PGR.
All: no training changes such as auxiliary confidence loss or ensembling.
All: no PGR as a function of supervisor or student size, task, or representations. Game Elo scaling is a different measure.
All: no weak-label fine-tuning failure modes. The Backdoor Code exploitation is induced by prompting in a monitoring game, not a student trained on weak labels.
All: the NSO theory concerns multi-step Guard win probability under Elo curves, not when a student trained on weak labels must beat its supervisor.
All: language models only, no vision.

record.verdict_notes: The rows correctly carry versions ['none']. Their states describe game scaling, not any claim version. The r7 state 'partial' reflects the 'nearly flat' Guard slope, which is fine as a description. The paper cites Burns et al. only in the introduction and related work.

versions.untested_parts: Strong-model fine-tuning on weak-model labels, beating the weak supervisor, and PGR.
Auxiliary confidence loss, weak-supervisor ensembling, loss variants, and their effects on PGR.
PGR variation with supervisor/student size, task, and representations. The paper measures game-based oversight performance against general Elo instead.
The specified failure modes for weak-label fine-tuning, including PGR under distribution shift and effects of shared errors.
Theory for when a student trained on weak labels must outperform its supervisor.
Weak-label fine-tuning outside language, including vision.

tranche.reason: Prompted oversight games measure game Elo scaling, without testing or using weak-label training gains. Section B explicitly leaves application to weak-label fine-tuning for future work.

source_check.notes: The four percentages are NSO projections from fitted Elo curves assuming no saturation, rather than measured multistep oversight outcomes. Debate has a 50% random-judge baseline.
